    PHATE and diffusion maps¶

    Python port of the R vignettes PHATE and Diffusion maps. Original author: Gregor Lueg.

    The diffusion family. Both model the data as a random walk over a kNN graph and both were built for continuous structure: trajectories, branch points, manifolds. PHATE lays out potential distances of the diffused walk with MDS, diffusion maps take the eigenvectors of the diffusion operator directly.

    In [1]:
    Copied! 
    import time
import warnings

warnings.filterwarnings("ignore", message="IProgress not found")

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import phate
import polars as pl
from sklearn.decomposition import PCA

import manifolds_rs as mf

pl.Config.set_fmt_str_lengths(60)


def scatter(
    ax: plt.Axes, emb: np.ndarray, c: np.ndarray, title: str, cmap: str = "tab10"
) -> None:
    """One embedding, coloured by `c`, without axis ticks."""
    ax.scatter(emb[:, 0], emb[:, 1], c=c, s=1, cmap=cmap, alpha=0.6)
    ax.set_title(title)
    ax.set_xticks([])
    ax.set_yticks([])


def panels(
    embeddings: dict[str, np.ndarray], c: np.ndarray, cmap: str = "tab10"
) -> None:
    """A row of embeddings sharing one colouring."""
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(
        1, len(embeddings), figsize=(4.3 * len(embeddings), 4.3), squeeze=False
    )
    for ax, (name, emb) in zip(axes[0], embeddings.items(), strict=True):
        scatter(ax, emb, c, name, cmap)
    fig.tight_layout()


def timed(fn) -> float:
    """Wall time of one call, in seconds."""
    start = time.perf_counter()
    fn()
    return time.perf_counter() - start
    import time import warnings warnings.filterwarnings("ignore", message="IProgress not found") import matplotlib.pyplot as plt import numpy as np import phate import polars as pl from sklearn.decomposition import PCA import manifolds_rs as mf pl.Config.set_fmt_str_lengths(60) def scatter( ax: plt.Axes, emb: np.ndarray, c: np.ndarray, title: str, cmap: str = "tab10" ) -> None: """One embedding, coloured by `c`, without axis ticks.""" ax.scatter(emb[:, 0], emb[:, 1], c=c, s=1, cmap=cmap, alpha=0.6) ax.set_title(title) ax.set_xticks([]) ax.set_yticks([]) def panels( embeddings: dict[str, np.ndarray], c: np.ndarray, cmap: str = "tab10" ) -> None: """A row of embeddings sharing one colouring.""" fig, axes = plt.subplots( 1, len(embeddings), figsize=(4.3 * len(embeddings), 4.3), squeeze=False ) for ax, (name, emb) in zip(axes[0], embeddings.items(), strict=True): scatter(ax, emb, c, name, cmap) fig.tight_layout() def timed(fn) -> float: """Wall time of one call, in seconds.""" start = time.perf_counter() fn() return time.perf_counter() - start

    PHATE¶

    PHATE runs in steps. An adaptive-bandwidth kernel over the kNN graph, shaped by decay, gives the affinities. Row-normalise and you have a Markov transition matrix, the diffusion operator. Power it to time t, picked at the knee of the von Neumann entropy unless you pin it. Diffusion denoises: local noise gets smoothed out and the global geometry comes forward. From the diffused transition probabilities PHATE computes a potential distance, the difference of their logs (gamma sets the exact transform), and lays it out with MDS.

    Against t-SNE and UMAP:

    • Built for continuous structure. Branching and continuous manifolds survive, where t-SNE and UMAP break them into islands.
    • Distances mean a bit more. The potential distance is a more interpretable metric than either of the others. Still don't over-read it.
    • Fails on genuinely discrete clusters. With no geometry connecting them, PHATE looks for a manifold that isn't there.
    • t matters. Too little diffusion and noise dominates, too much and the fine structure washes out. The entropy knee works well in practice, but look at what you get.
    In [2]:
    Copied! 
    X_clust, y_clust = mf.datasets.clustered(25_000)
X_swiss, t_swiss = mf.datasets.swiss_roll(1_000)
X_traj, y_traj = mf.datasets.trajectory(25_000)
order = np.random.default_rng(42).permutation(len(y_traj))
    X_clust, y_clust = mf.datasets.clustered(25_000) X_swiss, t_swiss = mf.datasets.swiss_roll(1_000) X_traj, y_traj = mf.datasets.trajectory(25_000) order = np.random.default_rng(42).permutation(len(y_traj))

    Clustered data¶

    The failure mode first, because it's worth seeing.

    In [3]:
    Copied! 
    panels(
    {"PCA": PCA(2).fit_transform(X_clust), "PHATE": mf.PHATE().fit_transform(X_clust)},
    y_clust,
)
    panels( {"PCA": PCA(2).fit_transform(X_clust), "PHATE": mf.PHATE().fit_transform(X_clust)}, y_clust, )

    The clusters get flung outwards and condensed into near points. PHATE is laying out a manifold that doesn't exist in this data. If yours looks like this, use t-SNE or UMAP.

    Swiss roll and trajectory¶

    In [4]:
    Copied! 
    panels(
    {
        "PCA": PCA(2).fit_transform(X_swiss),
        "PHATE": mf.PHATE().fit_transform(X_swiss),
    },
    t_swiss,
    cmap="viridis",
)
    panels( { "PCA": PCA(2).fit_transform(X_swiss), "PHATE": mf.PHATE().fit_transform(X_swiss), }, t_swiss, cmap="viridis", )
    In [5]:
    Copied! 
    panels(
    {
        "PCA": PCA(2).fit_transform(X_traj)[order],
        "PHATE": mf.PHATE().fit_transform(X_traj)[order],
    },
    y_traj[order],
)
    panels( { "PCA": PCA(2).fit_transform(X_traj)[order], "PHATE": mf.PHATE().fit_transform(X_traj)[order], }, y_traj[order], )

    This is the data PHATE was built for. The branches come out as branches, the progression along each one is kept and the branch points are where you would look for them.

    Pre-computed kNN graphs¶

    PHATE needs a wider graph than k: neighbours past the k-th join the kernel while their affinity clears the threshold, so the internal search runs 6 * k + 5 wide. Give a pre-computed graph the same width. With the graph fixed, pinning t is cheap to try.

    In [6]:
    Copied! 
    k = 5
idx, dist = mf.knn_graph(X_traj, k=6 * k + 5, ann="ivf")

panels(
    {
        f"t = {t}": mf.PHATE(k=k, t=t).fit_transform(
            X_traj, knn_indices=idx, knn_distances=dist
        )[order]
        for t in (None, 5, 50)
    },
    y_traj[order],
)
    k = 5 idx, dist = mf.knn_graph(X_traj, k=6 * k + 5, ann="ivf") panels( { f"t = {t}": mf.PHATE(k=k, t=t).fit_transform( X_traj, knn_indices=idx, knn_distances=dist )[order] for t in (None, 5, 50) }, y_traj[order], )

    t = None is the entropy knee, and it lands close to t = 5 here. At t = 50 the arcs straighten out and two of the early branches get squeezed into one line: fine structure washing out.

    Landmarks¶

    The full diffusion operator is N x N, and so is the dense potential distance matrix. Landmarks get around that: pick a representative subset, diffuse over it only, and interpolate everything else in. The default is 2048 landmarks (a power of two, for the SIMD in the k-means underneath). landmark_method picks them:

    • "spectral" (default): spectral clustering on the affinity graph. The most representative coverage on complex topology, and the most expensive.
    • "random": uniform. Fast, uneven coverage when the density varies.
    • "density": drawn by dampened node degree. A bit more careful than random, but rare branches can be missed.

    500 to 2000 landmarks cover most data up to a few hundred thousand points. Too few and the interpolation misses fine structure, too many and the speed advantage goes. n_landmarks=None runs the full operator, which gets nasty fast on large data.

    In [7]:
    Copied! 
    X_big, y_big = mf.datasets.trajectory(100_000)
order_big = np.random.default_rng(42).permutation(len(y_big))

panels(
    {
        f"landmarks: {m}": mf.PHATE(landmark_method=m).fit_transform(X_big)[order_big]
        for m in ("spectral", "random", "density")
    },
    y_big[order_big],
)
    X_big, y_big = mf.datasets.trajectory(100_000) order_big = np.random.default_rng(42).permutation(len(y_big)) panels( { f"landmarks: {m}": mf.PHATE(landmark_method=m).fit_transform(X_big)[order_big] for m in ("spectral", "random", "density") }, y_big[order_big], )

    Same tree three times, mirrored and rotated. With random landmarks the arms come out straighter, much like t = 50 above: the entropy knee is picked on the landmark operator, so it moves with the landmarks.

    Diffusion maps¶

    Same early pipeline as PHATE: a kNN graph, an adaptive Gaussian kernel, and an anisotropic normalisation (alpha) that corrects for uneven sampling. The result is a row-stochastic operator P, a random walk on the manifold. Then the paths split. Instead of diffusing for t steps and computing potential distances, diffusion maps eigendecompose the symmetric form of P. The top non-trivial eigenvectors are the coordinates, scaled by \(\lambda_k^t\), so t ends up as an exponent on the eigenvalues: larger t favours the dominant directions, smaller t keeps more detail.

    alpha is the distinctive knob. 0 gives the normalised graph Laplacian, 0.5 the Fokker-Planck operator, 1 (default) the Laplace-Beltrami operator, which recovers the manifold geometry independent of the sampling density.

    Against PHATE:

    • More transparent. The coordinates are eigenvectors of a well-defined operator, orthogonal and ordered by importance.
    • Different look. Axis-aligned, symmetric, horseshoes on linear trajectories where PHATE looks organic.
    • Different failure on clusters. With near-disconnected clusters the top eigenvectors approximate cluster indicators.
    • No MDS step, so the embedding is fixed once the operator is.
    In [8]:
    Copied! 
    panels(
    {
        "clusters": mf.DiffusionMaps().fit_transform(X_clust),
    },
    y_clust,
)
    panels( { "clusters": mf.DiffusionMaps().fit_transform(X_clust), }, y_clust, )

    Each cluster collapses to roughly one point: the eigenvectors are near constant within a cluster. PHATE shows the same problem less aggressively, because the log and the MDS keep a little spread. With ten near-disconnected components the spectrum has about ten eigenvalues close to 1, and two dimensions can't separate them all, hence the clusters crowding the middle. Diffusion maps collapsing harder than PHATE on your data is a signal in itself: it is more cluster than manifold. Reach for t-SNE, UMAP or PaCMAP.

    In [9]:
    Copied! 
    panels(
    {"swiss roll": mf.DiffusionMaps().fit_transform(X_swiss)},
    t_swiss,
    cmap="viridis",
)
    panels( {"swiss roll": mf.DiffusionMaps().fit_transform(X_swiss)}, t_swiss, cmap="viridis", )
    In [10]:
    Copied! 
    panels(
    {"trajectory": mf.DiffusionMaps().fit_transform(X_traj)[order]},
    y_traj[order],
)
    panels( {"trajectory": mf.DiffusionMaps().fit_transform(X_traj)[order]}, y_traj[order], )

    The swiss roll is the textbook case for diffusion maps, one of the canonical examples in the original paper. On the trajectory the branches come out as distinct directions, more orthogonal-looking than in PHATE. Both are valid pictures of the same structure.

    Pre-computed graphs work as everywhere else. With the graph fixed, iterate on alpha, t and bandwidth_scale at no search cost.

    In [11]:
    Copied! 
    idx_dm, dist_dm = mf.knn_graph(X_traj, k=5, ann="nndescent")

panels(
    {
        f"alpha = {a}": mf.DiffusionMaps(alpha=a).fit_transform(
            X_traj, knn_indices=idx_dm, knn_distances=dist_dm
        )[order]
        for a in (0.0, 0.5, 1.0)
    },
    y_traj[order],
)
    idx_dm, dist_dm = mf.knn_graph(X_traj, k=5, ann="nndescent") panels( { f"alpha = {a}": mf.DiffusionMaps(alpha=a).fit_transform( X_traj, knn_indices=idx_dm, knn_distances=dist_dm )[order] for a in (0.0, 0.5, 1.0) }, y_traj[order], )

    Landmarks¶

    The same landmark machinery as PHATE: pick a subset, eigendecompose the L x L landmark operator, Nystroem-extend back to everything. Unlike PHATE it is off by default. The full operator stays sparse and goes to a sparse eigensolver, while the landmark operator is dense, so on moderate data the full operator is the faster one. Landmarks are for data where the full operator no longer fits comfortably.

    In [12]:
    Copied! 
    dm_big = {
    "full operator": mf.DiffusionMaps(),
    "spectral landmarks": mf.DiffusionMaps(n_landmarks=2048),
    "random landmarks": mf.DiffusionMaps(n_landmarks=2048, landmark_method="random"),
}
dm_times = {}
dm_embs = {}
for name, est in dm_big.items():
    start = time.perf_counter()
    dm_embs[name] = est.fit_transform(X_big)[order_big]
    dm_times[name] = time.perf_counter() - start

panels(dm_embs, y_big[order_big])
pl.DataFrame(
    {"method": list(dm_times), "seconds": list(dm_times.values())}
).with_columns(pl.col("seconds").round(2))
    dm_big = { "full operator": mf.DiffusionMaps(), "spectral landmarks": mf.DiffusionMaps(n_landmarks=2048), "random landmarks": mf.DiffusionMaps(n_landmarks=2048, landmark_method="random"), } dm_times = {} dm_embs = {} for name, est in dm_big.items(): start = time.perf_counter() dm_embs[name] = est.fit_transform(X_big)[order_big] dm_times[name] = time.perf_counter() - start panels(dm_embs, y_big[order_big]) pl.DataFrame( {"method": list(dm_times), "seconds": list(dm_times.values())} ).with_columns(pl.col("seconds").round(2))
    Out[12]:
    shape: (3, 2)
    methodseconds
    strf64
    "full operator"1.07
    "spectral landmarks"3.66
    "random landmarks"1.26

    Timings on 100k points, one run each. The full operator wins, random landmarks come close, and the spectral selection costs several times more: it is there for the topology, not the speed.

    Benchmarks¶

    PHATE against the reference phate package, on all cores, one run each, wall time in seconds. Both run their defaults: k = 5, around 2000 landmarks, entropy-picked t.

    In [13]:
    Copied! 
    def bench(x: np.ndarray) -> pl.DataFrame:
    """Wall time of our PHATE and the reference on `x`."""
    runs = {
        "manifolds-rs PHATE spectral": lambda: mf.PHATE().fit_transform(x),
        "manifolds-rs PHATE random": lambda: mf.PHATE(
            landmark_method="random"
        ).fit_transform(x),
        "phate": lambda: phate.PHATE(
            n_jobs=-1, random_state=42, verbose=False
        ).fit_transform(x),
    }
    return pl.DataFrame(
        [{"method": k, "seconds": timed(fn)} for k, fn in runs.items()]
    ).with_columns(pl.col("seconds").round(2))


bench(mf.datasets.trajectory(10_000)[0])
    def bench(x: np.ndarray) -> pl.DataFrame: """Wall time of our PHATE and the reference on `x`.""" runs = { "manifolds-rs PHATE spectral": lambda: mf.PHATE().fit_transform(x), "manifolds-rs PHATE random": lambda: mf.PHATE( landmark_method="random" ).fit_transform(x), "phate": lambda: phate.PHATE( n_jobs=-1, random_state=42, verbose=False ).fit_transform(x), } return pl.DataFrame( [{"method": k, "seconds": timed(fn)} for k, fn in runs.items()] ).with_columns(pl.col("seconds").round(2)) bench(mf.datasets.trajectory(10_000)[0])

    Both the spectral and the random landmark versions beat the reference at both sizes, random by the widest margin. Neighbour search, kernel, diffusion time, potential distances and MDS all stay in Rust.
